result: Bioinformatic analysis of 120 bacterial INP sequences reveals that WO-coil counts vary considerably (30-70 coils, median 58), while R-coil counts are highly conserved (107 of 120 sequences contain either 10 or 12 R-coils). This stark difference in length variation supports the hypothesis that WO-coils and R-coils have different functions.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'A nice bioinformatics analysis that underscores that the hypothesis should apply not only to PbINP but to a wide range of (related) bacterial ice-nucleating proteins.' The editor notes the work provides 'solid evidence' and no reviewer challenges the bioinformatic findings.

result: The positively charged R-coil subdomain at the C-terminal end of the β-solenoid is crucial for multimerization and ice nucleation activity. Systematic deletion experiments show that reducing R-coils from 12 to 6 dramatically decreased activity (T50 = −35.7°C), and activity was entirely lost with only one R-coil remaining. Small decreases in R-coil length produce disproportionately large decreases in activity.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'The effects of mutations are really dramatic, so there is no doubt about the effect' and 'The variants tested are logical and progressively advance the story.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors use a rational mutagenesis approach to identify the role of the length, localisation, and amino acid composition of R-coils in ice nucleation activity.' The editor confirms 'solid evidence' from 'protein engineering experiments, functional assays.'

result: The location of R-coils at the C-terminal end next to the cap structure is critical for function. Relocating R-coils to the N-terminus reduced activity (T50 = −22.4°C), while midpoint relocation abolished activity (T50 = −36.1°C), indistinguishable from complete R-coil deletion.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'The variants tested are logical and progressively advance the story' and 'The effects of mutations are really dramatic, so there is no doubt about the effect.' No reviewer challenges these relocation experiments, which are part of the systematic mutagenesis approach praised by reviewers.

result: Electrostatic interactions between positively charged R-coils (Arg/Lys) and negatively charged WO-coils contribute to multimerization. Replacing R-coil arginines with acidic residues (RKH replacement) caused a 10.3°C drop in activity, while replacing arginines with lysines (K-coils) maintained wild-type activity (p=0.89), indicating that positive charge is more important than side chain geometry.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'The authors identify an underlying mechanism involving multimerization, which is plausible and compatible with EM data.' The editor notes the work details 'electrostatic interactions in the domain architecture of multimeric assemblies' with 'solid evidence.' No reviewer challenges the charge-swap experiments.

result: Cryo-electron tomography of recombinant E. coli shows that INP multimers form fibres ~5 nm across and up to 200 nm long. Wild-type INP-expressing cells appear lysed after cold acclimation and contain fibre clusters in the cytoplasm, while mutants lacking R-coils do not form these fibres and maintain intact cell envelopes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'The model is further shown to work in cells by tomography.' Reviewer 2 notes 'Convincing data that PbINP overexpressed in E coli forms fibrils (electron microscopy on E coli lysates).' The editor confirms 'solid evidence' from 'cryo-electron tomography.' However, Reviewer 2 notes a weakness: 'It is not shown however that the mutations that lead to loss of ice-nucleating activity also lead to loss of self-assembly.'

result: A structural model proposes that INP fibres consist of overlapping antiparallel dimers linked end-to-end through electrostatic interactions between R-coils and WO-coils. The model accounts for known properties including variable WO-coil lengths, heat stability, and the critical requirement for R-coils at the C-terminus.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'The theoretical model presented for how the proteins assemble into fibrils is simple, but not supported by much data.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the "working model" for the self-assembly of the fibers remains not more than that, just as in the earlier papers, since the mutation-activity relationship does not contain enough information to build a good structural model.' The editor explicitly states 'the proposed structural model of protein self-assembly remains hypothetical.'

result: Ice nucleation activity shows minimal pH dependence, with only modest decreases below pH 5.0 (~8°C loss at pH 2.0) and minimal loss up to pH 11.0. This pH insensitivity is reminiscent of antifreeze proteins and suggests the water-organizing mechanism is not pH-dependent.
evaluation: No reviewer challenges the pH stability data. The experiments are part of the 'solid evidence' from 'functional assays' noted by the editor. The finding supports the proposed mechanism and is consistent with prior literature.

result: INP multimers exhibit remarkable heat resistance, retaining most activity even after heating to 99°C for 10 min (only 5°C activity loss), while the GFP control denatures at 75°C. Heat resistance is not affected by WO-coil truncation, suggesting R-coils and the C-terminal cap are mainly responsible for multimer stability.
evaluation: No reviewer challenges the heat stability data. The experiments are part of the 'solid evidence' from 'functional assays' noted by the editor. The finding supports the proposed role of R-coils in multimer stability.

result: The N-terminal domain is not essential for ice nucleation activity (no difference between truncations and wild-type, p=0.82), while the highly conserved C-terminal cap is essential. A triple mutant disrupting the cap structure (F1204D, D1208L, Y1230D) showed greatly reduced activity (T50 = −27.8°C), validating the AlphaFold-predicted cap structure.
evaluation: No reviewer challenges these findings. The experiments are part of the systematic mutagenesis approach praised by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes 'The variants tested are logical and progressively advance the story.'

result: Filtered bacterial lysate supernatant retains high ice nucleation activity (T50 = −9.6°C), only a few degrees lower than whole bacteria, indicating that large INP structures are present within the bacterial cytoplasm.
evaluation: No reviewer challenges this finding. It supports the self-assembly hypothesis and is consistent with the cryo-ET observations. The editor notes 'solid evidence' from functional assays.
